en_O01: A fifty-year-old man fell down the stairs. His lower leg is very painful and swollen, and he cannot put weight on it. The X-ray shows a fracture with the bone pieces out of place.
en_O02: In fracture fixation surgery, the surgeon lines up the pieces of bone and holds them together with metal: a plate with screws, separate screws, a rod inside the bone, or wires. The implant holds the pieces in the right position while the bone heals by itself.
en_O03: The surgeon decides based on the examination and X-rays. Surgery may be offered if the bone pieces are badly out of place, the fracture is unstable, or the joint surface is damaged and needs to be restored to its proper shape. Many fractures that are not out of place are treated without surgery: with a cast, a brace or a bandage.
en_O04: If there is a wound near the fracture, even a small one, the fracture may be open, and the bone does not have to be visible. Do not wash out a deep wound or push a sticking-out bone back yourself. Cover the wound with a clean dressing and call one-zero-one straight away.
en_O05: The limb is held in a splint or cast and kept raised. Staff regularly check the colour, warmth, feeling and movement of your fingers or toes. Tell staff straight away if the pain suddenly gets much worse, or if you notice numbness, tingling, or cold, pale or bluish fingers or toes. If you have ever had an allergy to metal, especially nickel, tell your surgeon.
en_O06: The operation is done under a general or regional anaesthetic; the anaesthetist will explain the choice. X-rays are taken during surgery to check the position of the bone pieces and the metal. The cut is closed with stitches or staples.
en_O07: Keep the operated arm or leg raised and move your fingers or toes. Only put weight or load on the limb as your surgeon allows: too much too early can move the bone pieces or break the implant. A physiotherapist will teach you to walk with a frame or crutches.
en_O08: Take your painkillers as prescribed and do not add medicines on your own. After a leg fracture the risk of blood clots goes up, so the team decides whether you need preventive treatment. Not everyone gets it. Do not stop or add these medicines yourself.
en_O09: The bone takes several weeks or months to heal, sometimes longer. The pain may go before the bone is strong enough, so come to your follow-up visits and X-rays. Keep the wound clean and change the dressing as staff have shown you.
en_O10: Plates, screws and rods are often left in the bone if they cause no problems; your surgeon will decide whether removal is needed. Before an MRI scan, always tell staff that you have metal in your body. If the fracture happened after a minor fall, talk to your family doctor about testing for osteoporosis.
en_O11: For sudden shortness of breath or chest pain, call one-zero-one. If you have severe pain that keeps getting worse, especially if it does not ease after a painkiller or gets worse when you move your fingers or toes, or you have numbness, cold, pale or bluish fingers or toes, or the cast is pressing hard, you need emergency help at once. Do not drive yourself. If you cannot get to the emergency department quickly and safely, call an ambulance on one-zero-one. A temperature of thirty-eight degrees or more, redness, swelling or discharge from the wound, or new pain or swelling in the calf: see a doctor the same day.
en_O12: These are general recommendations. Individual instructions from your doctor and medical team come first.
